deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. The main content is a complete, numbered (1 to 120) table of words of length 10 over the letters a to e, in which each letter occurs exactly twice. The words are normalised so that letters first appear in the order a, b, c, d, e.

The defining property can be checked on every legible entry: between the two occurrences of any letter there is an even number of letters. This is Gauss's parity condition for the sequence of crossings met while traversing a closed plane curve with 5 double points (a 'Gauss word' or 'Gauss code'). In modern terms the table is the set of linear chord diagrams with 5 chords in which every chord crosses an even number of other chords; equivalently, the interlacement graph is Eulerian.

The pen sketches in the middle of the sheet support this reading. They are closed self-intersecting curves (knot-like diagrams), some with small letters at the crossings. The right-hand sideways column carries further words of the same kind (e.g. aa…) and the Roman numerals I to VIII. The numerals belong to the unrelated 4% discounting computation on the next page (25·0.9615384…; 0.9615384 = 1/1.04). The left margin is a list of Göttingen names (Lichtenberg, Blumenbach, Heeren, Tychsen, Harding, Grotefend(?) …), numbered 1 to 9, with the dates 1800 and 1810. It is non-mathematical.

STRUCTURE OF THE ENUMERATION (lexicographic order, with Gauss's own repairs):
- 1 to 24: words aa·W, where W runs through all 24 admissible 4-letter words (on b to e).
- 25 to 30: abba·W, with W one of the 6 admissible 3-letter words. The 3-letter list is ccddee, ccdeed, cddcee, cddeec, cdecde, cdeedc.
- 31 to 44, plus inserted 45* to 48*: prefix abca…, 18 words. Gauss first skipped the abcade… block. He then wrote it in at the head of column 3 as 45* to 48* (abcadebced, abcadebdec, abcadeecbd, abcadeedbc). He marked the insertion point with a star and renumbered the following entries by +4.
- 49 to 54: abccb…, 6 words.
- 55 to 66: abccd…, 12 words: abccdabdee, abccdabeed, abccdaedbe, abccdaeebd, abccddbaee, abccddbeea, abccddeabe, abccddeeba, abccdebaed, abccdebdea, abccdeeabd, abccdeedba.
- 67 to 102: prefix abcd…, 36 words, in three blocks:
  - 67 to 78, abcdb…: e.g. abcdbadcee, abcdbcdaee, and abcdbedaec, abcdbedcea, abcdbeeadc, abcdbeecda.
  - 79 to 90, abcdd…: e.g. abcddabcee … abcddeecba.
  - 91 to 102, abcde…: abcdeabcde, abcdeabedc, abcdeadcbe, abcdeadebc, abcdecbade, abcdecbeda, abcdecdabe, abcdecdeba, abcdeebadc, abcdeebcda, abcdeedabc, abcdeedcba.
- 103 to 120: the forgotten class abbc…, 18 words, appended at the end. Within it the subclass abbccde… (119, 120) was itself added last.

Tally (my addition): 24 + 6 + 18 + 18 + 18 + 36 = 120. The class counts reflect a recursion visible in Gauss's arrangement:
- words beginning aa: N(4) = 24;
- all other words: 96 = 4·24.

The smaller cases fit the same pattern: N(1..5) = 1, 2, 6, 24, 120 = n!, with N(n) − N(n−1) = (n−1)·N(n−1). I verified N(3) = 6 and N(4) = 24 by hand. N(4) = 24 splits as 14 non-crossing diagrams, 8 with interlacement graph triangle + isolated chord, and 2 with graph C4 (abcadcbd, abcdbadc). The page itself states no count or formula.

THE STARS (my interpretation). Entries 35 (abcabdecde) and 39 (abcadcedbe) carry an asterisk.
- No. 35's interlacement graph is two triangles sharing the vertex c (a bowtie).
- No. 39's graph is the 5-cycle a-b-e-d-c-a.

Both satisfy the parity condition, yet both fail the planarity (realisability) criterion. For example, in no. 39 the non-interlaced pair a, e has exactly one common neighbour (b). In no. 35 the non-interlaced pair a, d has only c as common neighbour. In Rosenstiehl's characterisation, non-interlaced pairs must have an even number of common neighbours. So these words are not Gauss words of plane curves. It is plausible (not certain) that Gauss's stars mark them as parity-admissible but not drawable. That would mean he saw that his parity condition is not sufficient. The star at 45 is an insertion mark.

The sketched curves are presumably his attempts to realise words.
errors: Apart from the omissions Gauss himself repaired (the abcade… block, inserted as 45*–48* with renumbering; the abbc… class, appended as 103–120; the abbccde… subclass, added as 119–120), no entry I could check violates the parity condition, and the class sizes add up to exactly 120.

Several words in the supplied machine transcription violate the condition (e.g. no. 5 'aabbcdeede', no. 35 'abcabdeede', no. 75 'bedace', the 55–66 block). These are transcription misreadings (c read as e, a dropped c, etc.), not Gauss's errors.

Whether every starred/unstarred word is correctly classified as realizable is not checkable from the page. Other words with C5 or bowtie interlacement graphs, if present and unstarred, would show the stars are not a complete realizability marking.

results.what: Complete enumeration of all 120 normalized double-occurrence words on 5 letters satisfying the even-interval (Gauss parity) condition, i.e. candidate crossing sequences of closed plane curves with 5 double points
results.modern_name: Gauss codes / even (Eulerian-interlacement) linear chord diagrams; enumeration of Gauss words
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (parity condition, Nachlass, Werke VIII 'Zur Geometrie der Lage'); systematic enumeration of curve codes in later knot-tabulation work (Tait, Kirkman 1870s–80s)

results.what: Implicit recursive count N(n)=1,2,6,24,120 (aa-prefixed class N(n-1), remainder (n-1)·N(n-1)), i.e. n! even linear chord diagrams on n chords
results.modern_name: Counting even (all-crossing-degrees-even) linear chord diagrams; equals n! (my verification for n≤5)

results.what: Starring of nos. 35 and 39, which satisfy the parity condition but are not planar Gauss words (bowtie and C5 interlacement graphs). This possibly indicates awareness that the parity condition is insufficient.
results.modern_name: Non-realizable Gauss codes; realizability criteria (Rosenstiehl 1976, de Fraysseix–Ossona de Mendez)
results.usually_credited_to: Insufficiency usually credited to Nagy (1927) / Dehn (1936); full characterization Rosenstiehl (1976)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's work on Gauss codes and his parity condition is well known from Werke VIII and from Epple's studies, so the topic is not surprising. Two things are notable unpublished details. First, a complete, carefully repaired table of all 120 five-crossing parity words, whose structure exhibits n!. Second, the stars on exactly two parity-admissible but non-planar words (35 and 39). If confirmed to mark non-realizability, the stars would show early awareness of the insufficiency of the parity condition.
